title: Abdali's invasions
hook: Ahmad Shah Abdali came down through Punjab again and again

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy raised on kirtan grew into Sultan-ul-Qaum. Your line was leader of the qaum. Today the week ends, with a storm that kept coming back.

Dust on the road from the northwest. A farmer in Punjab straightens up in his field and watches it. He has seen this before. A huge army is coming down out of Afghanistan, across the rivers, heading for the riches of Delhi. It will pass through his land on the way there and on the way back. And then, some time later, the dust will rise again. The king at the head of that army was Ahmad Shah Abdali, and Punjab lay across his road.
screen: `DUST FROM THE NORTHWEST.` → `AN ARMY BOUND FOR DELHI.` → `AND THEN IT COMES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Abdali was the king of Afghanistan, and he invaded northern India again and again. Each time, his army marched through Punjab. For the people there, that meant crops taken, towns emptied, captives carried off. Then the army went home, the land tried to recover, and the army came back. So the Sikhs' question wasn't how to win one battle. It was how to keep going through a storm that returns. Tradition and history describe their answer. The Dal Khalsa mostly didn't meet the full army head on. They let it pass, and struck its edges and its rear, especially on the way home, when it was heavy with plunder and captives, the same tactic the riders used on Nadir Shah's army this week. And when the army left, they came out of the forests and took the countryside again. Sikhs have a phrase for that spirit, one this path met in the forests, and it comes in the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of gurdwara gatherings: chardi kala. Rising spirits, a spirit that keeps climbing. The Ardas asks that through the Name there be chardi kala. It isn't cheerfulness. It's the refusal to stay knocked down. Look back at this week through that lens. A father and son who would not give up their faith. Captives brought home. Grief held without hate. Villages kept safe. Scattered bands made one army, and a leader who carried his people. Each was a way of standing up again. Abdali came again and again. So did they.
screen: `A KING WHO KEPT COMING BACK.` · `STRIKE THE EDGES, THEN RETURN.` · `CHARDI KALA: RISING SPIRITS.` · `A WEEK OF STANDING UP AGAIN.` · then, large: `AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that keeps coming back in your life, a Sunday-night worry, an argument that circles round, and let yourself be tired of it; that's allowed. Then breathe in with the word again, and out with and again, not as a complaint but as standing up one more time. If you pray, say Waheguru instead.
Abdali's invasions. The Afghan king's armies came through Punjab again and again, and the Khalsa met each return by returning too, in the spirit the Ardas calls chardi kala. Today's word.
Your line: again and again. Rising spirits are built one return at a time. Rest well; a new week starts tomorrow.
